mcqs.question: Why is distinguishing a crashed node from a slow node fundamental to why consensus is hard?
options: A node waiting for a response can't tell whether to keep waiting (the other node is just slow) or treat it as failed and move on, and guessing wrong risks two nodes disagreeing about the outcome
Crashed nodes and slow nodes always use different network ports
It isn't actually relevant — consensus protocols simply ignore node failures
Only crashed nodes matter; slow nodes have no effect on consensus protocols
mcqs.explanation: The inability to reliably tell "slow" from "dead" is exactly the core difficulty consensus protocols must handle without ever getting it wrong in a way that causes disagreement. It's not about network ports, and both slow and crashed nodes matter — protocols must handle both correctly.

mcqs.question: Why does a consensus-backed decision typically cost at least one network round trip more than a single node just deciding on its own?
options: The decision isn't considered final until it's confirmed by a majority of nodes, which requires waiting on responses from other machines
Consensus protocols always retry every request three times regardless of outcome
It's a limitation of Raft specifically, not consensus protocols in general
Network round trips are unrelated to why consensus is slower
mcqs.explanation: Needing majority confirmation before a decision is final is exactly what adds the round-trip cost compared to a single node deciding unilaterally. It's not an arbitrary triple-retry rule, it isn't Raft-specific (Paxos has the same majority requirement), and round trips are precisely the mechanism at play.

mcqs.question: In Raft, when is a log entry considered committed?
options: As soon as the leader appends it to its own local log
As soon as any single follower acknowledges it
Once a majority of nodes (including the leader) have durably stored the entry
Only after every node in the cluster has stored it, with no exceptions
mcqs.explanation: Raft commits an entry once a majority — not just the leader alone, not just any one follower, and not necessarily every single node — has durably stored it. That majority threshold is what lets the system tolerate a minority of nodes failing.

mcqs.question: A system needs to store millions of independent shopping-cart records with high write throughput, tolerating occasional conflicts that get resolved after the fact. Which approach fits better: consensus or quorum-based storage?
options: Consensus, since it guarantees no two writes ever conflict
Neither approach can handle high write volume
Consensus, because it has higher throughput than quorum-based storage
Quorum-based storage, since it allows conflicts to happen and resolves them without needing every write to go through majority agreement
mcqs.explanation: Quorum-based storage is built exactly for this: high-volume independent writes with conflicts resolved afterward, without the majority-agreement bottleneck consensus requires for every decision. Consensus doesn't eliminate conflicts in this data pattern and has lower throughput here, not higher, and both approaches can handle high volume in their respective niches.

mcqs.question: A team routes every write of a high-volume, independent key-value dataset through a Raft-backed consensus log, believing it's the safest option. What's the likely downside?
options: Every write now pays a majority round-trip cost that a well-tuned quorum could have avoided for a workload that could tolerate resolving occasional conflicts
There is no downside — consensus is strictly better than a quorum for any kind of data
Consensus doesn't support key-value data at all
The data becomes permanently unreadable once written through consensus
mcqs.explanation: Consensus is stronger than needed here and pays for it in throughput — a tuned quorum would have handled this high-volume, conflict-tolerant workload with less overhead. Consensus is not universally better for every data shape, it can absolutely store key-value data, and nothing about it makes data unreadable.
